source.title_on_document: Putting GPT-3's Creativity to the (Alternative Uses) Test

supplement.where: http://osf.io/vmk3c/ (p. 3, Results; also osf.io/vmk3c/ on p. 2, Materials)
supplement.holds: Data, code, Dutch-to-English translations, data cleaning steps, rating protocols, categorization protocols, and the Monte Carlo prompt/parameter optimization studies. The main text reports regression coefficients with SEs and test statistics, but does not tabulate exact group means or SDs. Figures 2 to 5 are bar charts; Figure 6 is a violin plot with boxplots of flexibility scores (PDF pp. 3-4).

paper_design_summary: The authors compare Alternative Uses Test (AUT) responses for book, fork, and tin can from 42 University of Amsterdam students (previously collected, in Dutch, translated to English) with responses from 144 runs of GPT-3 (davinci-002). Blinded trained judges rated each response on originality, utility, and surprise; semantic distance from the object was computed with spaCy embeddings, and flexibility of tin-can response sets was coded by category. No participant used AI.

studies.label: GPT-3 vs. student responses on the Alternative Uses Test

participants.exclusions: Human side: 823 responses from 42 students; after removing invalid and incomplete responses, 774 human responses analyzed. GPT-3 side (not people): 820 responses from 144 runs; 781 analyzed.
participants.who: Human arm: students from the University of Amsterdam fluent in Dutch, previously collected data, received study credits. Comparison arm: 144 GPT-3 runs of the AUT.
participants.quote: The human sample comprised of previously collected data of 823 responses from 42 students from the University of Amsterdam.

ai_tool.how_used: GPT-3 produced AUT responses itself through the API (temperature sampled from .65 to .80, frequency and presence penalty 1), with a prompt chosen by Monte Carlo optimization; 820 responses collected over two sessions. No human used AI (p. 2, Materials).

task.description: Alternative Uses Test for 'Book', 'Fork', and 'Tin Can': list as many creative uses as possible.
task.duration: Humans: two minutes per object (p. 2, Materials)

outcomes.name: Originality rating
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained judges, blinded to source, rated each response on a 5-point scale; ICC = .78 after removing invalid responses. Hierarchical regression at the response level with a human versus GPT-3 contrast plus AUT object; positive beta = humans higher.

contrasts.reported: humans had higher originality (β=.17, SE = .06, z = 2.91, p = .004) [beta is the human versus GPT-3 contrast; n_units 1555 = 774 human + 781 GPT-3 responses as printed]

outcomes.name: Utility rating
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained blinded judges, 5-point scale; ICC = .70 after cleaning. Same hierarchical regression.

contrasts.reported: GPT-3 had higher utility ratings (β=-.55, SE = .06, z = -8.52, p<.001)

outcomes.name: Surprise rating
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained blinded judges, 5-point scale; ICC = .79 after cleaning. Same hierarchical regression.

contrasts.reported: humans had higher ... surprise (β=.14, SE = .07, z = 1.96, p = .050) ratings

outcomes.name: Semantic distance from the AUT object
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: 1 minus cosine similarity between the response embedding and the object embedding (spaCy en_core_web_lg). Same hierarchical regression.

contrasts.reported: as well as larger semantic distance scores (β= .10, SE = . 02, z = 5.45, p<.001) than GPT-3

outcomes.name: Flexibility of response set (tin can only)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of pre-defined categories in a response set divided by the number of responses; one judge per object categorized responses. Computed on tin-can data only. Each unit is one response set (one student or one GPT-3 run); the paper does not print the number of sets.

contrasts.reported: Humans had, on average, higher flexibility scores (F(1, 85) = 5.53, p = .021). ... GPT-3's flexibility scores show greater variance.

eligibility.reason: GPT-3's own AUT responses are compared with previously collected responses of 42 students; no person received AI help and nobody was assigned to AI (p. 2, Methods).

one_line_finding: Students' Alternative Uses Test responses were rated more original (beta = .17, SE = .06, p = .004) and more surprising (beta = .14, SE = .07, p = .050), had larger semantic distance (beta = .10, SE = .02, p < .001), and had higher tin-can flexibility (F(1, 85) = 5.53, p = .021) than GPT-3's responses, while GPT-3's responses were rated more useful (beta = -.55, SE = .06, p < .001) (p. 3, Results).
notes: The ICC sentence on p. 2 refers to 'approximately 10% of the 1656 responses', while the sample counts give 823 human + 820 GPT-3 = 1643 responses before cleaning; the paper does not explain the gap. Coefficients are a human versus GPT-3 contrast (positive = humans higher). Arm means appear only as bar charts by object (Figures 2 to 5).
